The “Input Records” table appears in Chapter 2 (“Input Description”) of the DBMERG Manual (Service Pack 2025-4, Build 146). Its sole purpose is to enumerate every available record (or keyword block) that DBMERG recognizes when reading an instruction file. Below is a structured breakdown of that table:

1. Table context  
   • Location  
     – Chapter 2, Section 2.2 “Input Records” (starts on page 2-1)  
   • Purpose  
     – Provides a one‐line entry for each DBMERG record type  
     – Associates a code (keyword), a brief name, and the page on which its full syntax and parameter list are defined  

2. Columns of the table  
   • Section Number  
     – A hierarchical section ID (e.g. 2.3, 2.4.1, 2.5, …)  
     – Indicates where in Chapter 2 the detailed description of that record lives  
   • Record Name (Keyword)  
     – A short, uppercase mnemonic (e.g. CDB, CTRL, LC, GRP, NODE, BEAM, TRUS, CABL, SPRI, QUAD, BRIC, EXTR, ECHO)  
     – This is the token the user places at the start of a record in the input file  
   • Description  
     – A concise title explaining the record’s function  
     – Examples:  
       • “Selection of a database” for CDB  
       • “Control options” for CTRL  
       • “Group Assignment” for GRP  
       • “Plane Elements” for QUAD  
   • Page Reference  
     – The page in the manual where the record’s full syntax, parameter definitions, default values, and examples are provided (e.g. pages 2-2 through 2-15)  

3. List of Records and Their Roles  
   2.1 Input Language  
     – General syntax rules, comment conventions, line continuations  
   2.2 Input Records  
     – This summary table itself  
   2.3 CDB – Selection of a database  
     – Specifies source (“.cdb”) and target project database  
   2.4 CTRL – Control options  
     – Global switches (verbose mode, restart-control via 2.4.1 REST)  
   2.5 LC – Load Cases  
     – Defines or remaps load‐case identifiers during merge  
   2.6 GRP – Group Assignment  
     – How elements/nodes are matched between source and target via group IDs  
   2.7 NODE – Nodal Values  
     – Import or modify nodal loads/results  
   2.8 BEAM – Beam Elements  
     – Distribute or remap beam‐element results/properties  
   2.9 TRUS – Truss Elements  
     – Same purpose as BEAM but for truss members  
   2.10 CABL – Cable Elements  
     – Cable‐element-specific data mapping  
   2.11 SPRI – Spring Elements  
     – Spring‐element-specific data mapping  
   2.12 QUAD – Plane Elements  
     – Shell/plate‐element data  
   2.13 BRIC – 3D Continua Elements  
     – Solid‐element data  
   2.14 EXTR – Data mapping 2D–3D  
     – Projection or interpolation of 2D results into 3D continua  
   2.15 ECHO – Volume of Output  
     – Controls echoing of processed records back into the report file  

4. How to use this table in RAG/Vector‐Store ingestion  
   • Index each record entry as a separate document or facet  
   • Store the keyword, section number, and short description as searchable fields  
   • Link each keyword to its detailed syntax page for quick drill-down during retrieval  
   • Tag the records by element type (nodal, beam, truss, etc.) to support filtered queries  

In sum, this “Input Records” table is a high‐level index into all of DBMERG’s input commands, grouping them by functionality (database selection, control flags, load cases, grouping rules, element‐specific data) and pointing users to the exact manual pages where each command is defined in full.

 1 Task Description
 Program DBMERG allows the modification or transfer of data within a data base or between data bases of the SOFiSTiK-Software. The program may be used for merging results from different tasks, the treatment of multiple used parts or the transfer of primary load states.
 The program has functions as follows:
 Import of loads or results
 - Distribution or results or properties of elements

Program DBMERG allows the modification or transfer of data within a data base or between data bases of the SOFiSTiK-Software. The program may be used for merging results from different tasks, the treatment of multiple used parts or the transfer of primary load states.. The program has functions as follows:. Import of loads or results. - Distribution or results or properties of elements.
 - Changing results with factors
 These functions require a special responsability of the user, because the check of those results may become extremely difficult.
 DBMERG uses one or two SOFiSTiK-databases, each of them needs a static system. When calling the program a second data base will be opened with the name of the input file. This will be the source, while the project data base is the target.
 Elements and nodes of the project data base will be assigned to those in the source data base via groups and load cases. Grouping within DBMERG extends beyond the general SOFiSTiK group mechanisms.
 DBMERG will copy all results from the source to the target and will replace load cases and or element or node numbers.
The input occurs in a free format with the CADINP input language (see the general manual SOFiSTiK: ’FEA / STRUCTURAL Installation and Basics’).

Below is a structured, self-contained description of the input table. It explains the overall context (block structure, record delimiters) and then walks through each record type and its allowed items. You can index this summary in your RAG vector store to answer questions about record syntax, item names or grouping.

1. General Block Organization  
- Input is divided into one or more “blocks.”  
- Every block must end with the record END.  
- An empty block (i.e. an immediate END/END) signals the end of all input.  
- Within one block only a single external database may be referenced.  
- Standard records HEAD, END and PAGE are defined in the SOFiSTiK manual “FEA / STRUCTURAL Installation and Basics.”

2. Record-to-Items Mapping  
Each record in the table has a fixed name and a specific set of fields (items) that may appear on its line. These items govern what data the record carries.

A. Database Control and Group Definitions  
• CDB  
 – FROM: Starting database number or handle  
 – PASS: Pass identifier or sequence number  

• MAT (Material Ranges)  
• SECT (Section Ranges)  
Both share the same set of items used to generate sequential definitions:  
 – FROM: First index in the range  
 – TO: Last index  
 – INC: Increment step  
 – BY: Optional multiplier or grouping  

• LC (Load Case Grouping)  
 – NO: Load case number  
 – NOS: Number of load cases  

• GRP (General Grouping)  
 – NO: Group number  
 – NOS: Number of entries in that group  

B. Nodal and Element-Based Load Definitions  
These records assign loads or boundary conditions to structural objects.

• NODE (Nodal Supports / Reactions)  
 – TYPE: Load type code (e.g., fixed, pinned)  
 – FX, FY, FZ: Force components in X/Y/Z directions  
 – FXX, FYY, FZZ: Moment (couple) components about X/Y/Z axes  

• BEAM (Beam-Element End Loads)  
 – TYPE: Load distribution type (e.g., uniform, triangular)  
 – FN: Axial force  
 – FVY, FVZ: Shear forces in local Y and Z  
 – FMT, FMY, FMZ: Moments about local axes  
 – FMB: Warping moment or bimoment  

• TRUS (Truss Element)  
• CABL (Cable Element)  
• SPRI (Spring Element)  
All three share:  
 – TYPE: Load or support type code  
 – FN: Axial force  

C. Surface and Solid Element Loads  
• QUAD (Quadrilateral Shell/Plate Element)  
 – TYPE: Load type code  
 – FMX, FMY: Membrane forces in X and Y  
 – FMXY: Membrane shear resultants  
 – FVX, FVY: Transverse shear resultants in X/Y  
 – FNX, FNY: Normal pressure on two opposing faces  
 – FNXY: Bi-directional normal pressure shear  

• BRIC (Brick / Solid Element)  
 – TYPE: Load type code  
 – FSX, FSY, FSZ: Surface loads on faces normal to X, Y, Z  
 – FTAU: Tangential shear load on face  

D. Auxiliary Output Control  
• ECHO  
 – OPT: Option keyword controlling what is echoed back to output  
 – VAL: Associated value or flag  

3. Usage Notes for RAG Indexing  
- Each record name (e.g. NODE, BEAM) forms a top-level key.  
- The list of items under that key enumerates permissible parameters.  
- Lookups can answer “which items can I supply on a QUAD record?” or “what fields define a NODE support?”  
- The grouping into A, B, C, D above reflects logical families: global controls, ranges, line loads, surface/solid loads, and output directives.

 The records HEAD, END and PAGE are described in the general manual SOFiSTiK: ’FEA / STRUCTURAL Installation and Basics’.

The table you’ve provided defines two parameters—FROM and PASS—that are used by the CDB “merge” command to specify and access an external database during an import or merge operation. Below is a detailed, structured description of each column and row, along with how these parameters fit into the overall CDB workflow.

1. Overall Table Structure  
   • Columns  
     – Item: the keyword or parameter name recognized by the CDB merge command.  
     – Description: a concise explanation of the role or meaning of that parameter.  
     – Unit: the data type and maximum length allowed for the parameter value.  
     – Default: the default or placeholder value taken if the parameter is omitted or uses a special indicator.  
   • Rows  
     – Two rows correspond to two possible parameters: FROM and PASS. Each parameter may appear at most once in each “input block” of the CDB command.  

2. Context of Use  
   • The CDB merge command is designed to import or merge records from a source database into the “master project.”  
   • You can define a source database with the FROM parameter; if you omit an explicit path and provide only a record name, CDB assumes the master project’s database.  
   • The PASS parameter is used only when that source database is password-protected—otherwise it can be left blank or omitted.  

3. Detailed Parameter Breakdown  
   A. FROM  
     – Description: “File name of a database.”  
     – Role: Identifies the file path or database identifier to be used as the source for import/merge. This could be a local path, network path, or any CDB-recognized database alias.  
     – Unit (Lit256): A literal string token with a maximum length of 256 characters. This allows for reasonably long file paths or descriptive database names.  
     – Default (!): The exclamation mark serves as a special token. In practice, it signals that no custom database path was supplied and that the “master project” database should be used. In many CDB implementations, “!” is a shorthand for “current project’s database.”  
   B. PASS  
     – Description: “Optional password for protected database.”  
     – Role: Supplies the password needed to unlock or authenticate against the source database, if encryption or access control is enabled.  
     – Unit (Lit16): A literal string of up to 16 characters. This limit balances basic password complexity without encouraging excessively long secrets.  
     – Default (–): A hyphen indicates a blank or null password. If the database has no password, you can omit this parameter or supply “–” to explicitly signal “no password.”  

4. Constraints and Best Practices  
   • Each parameter (FROM and PASS) may appear only once per input block. Attempting to redefine the same parameter in the same block will result in an error.  
   • If you specify only a record name for FROM (no path), CDB will treat that as part of the master project—so always use the full file name if you intend to pull from an entirely separate database.  
   • Because passwords are sensitive, ensure that PASS is handled securely: avoid logging it in plaintext, and use environment variables or secure credential stores where possible.  

5. How This Description Supports RAG Vector Stores  
   • By capturing parameter semantics, defaults, and data-type constraints in a structured description, a Retrieval-Augmented Generation system can answer questions like:  
     – “What is the default behavior when no source database is specified?”  
     – “Which parameter do I use to unlock an encrypted CDB database?”  
   • This metadata is easily converted into key-value pairs or vector embeddings for rapid lookup and natural-language Q&A in documentation assistants.

CDB
 For the merging this command selects a database to be used as source for any import. If the record name is given only, the master project will be used again. A definition is only possible once in every input block.

CTRL
 Item Description Unit Default OPT One of the following options: LT - REST restart control

By defualt, possibly existing results of the target load case are deleted pior to copying.
 The restart option CTRL REST 1 suppresses deletion of load case dependent data (results) for the target load case. This allows, e.g., to realize different mapping rules (GRP ...) for nodal results and elemental results in subsequent DBMERG runs.

The table at hand defines the two primary input parameters you must supply when invoking the DBMERG “HEAD GRP” command sequence for load-case result transfers.  It consists of four columns—Item, Description, Unit and Default—and two rows corresponding to the parameters NO and NOS.  Here is a breakdown of each field:

1. Columns  
   • Item  
     – The mnemonic or keyword you type into the DBMERG command.  
   • Description  
     – A brief human-readable explanation of what value this keyword represents.  
   • Unit  
     – The measurement unit for the value.  A dash (“–”) indicates that these parameters are pure indices or identifiers, not physical quantities.  
   • Default  
     – The value assumed if you omit the parameter from your input.  An asterisk (*) denotes that the parameter has no implicit default and must be provided explicitly; referring back to another field (as with NOS) indicates that the default is “copy from the NO parameter.”

2. Rows / Parameters  
   1. NO  
      • Description: “New load case number”  
      • Unit: – (no unit)  
      • Default: *  
        – The asterisk here means NO is mandatory.  You must tell DBMERG which target load-case number you want to receive the merged or copied results.  
   2. NOS  
      • Description: “Old load case number”  
      • Unit: – (no unit)  
      • Default: NO  
        – If you do not explicitly specify NOS, the system assumes you want to copy from the same load case number that you just declared as NO.  By default, old and new load-case numbers coincide unless you override NOS.

3. How They Fit into DBMERG Workflows  
   • During a DBMERG run, you typically specify a sequence of blocks such as  
       +PROG DBMERG  
         HEAD  
           GRP  
             NO   <new-LC>  
             NOS  <old-LC>  
           END  
       ENDPROG  
   • In simple 1-to-1 transfers, you’d set NO = 10, NOS = 5, meaning “copy results from load case 5 into load case 10.”  
   • If you omit NOS, DBMERG takes NOS=NO and effectively does a no-op (overwrites LC n with LC n), useful when combined with grouping rules to multiply or redistribute results among structural parts.  
   • Because both NO and NOS carry no physical units, they act purely as database indices.  NO must always be defined; NOS defaults to matching NO.

4. Practical Implications  
   • Mandatory vs. Optional  
     – NO: mandatory.  You cannot run a HEAD GRP step without a target (new) load case number.  
     – NOS: optional.  Defaults to the same number as NO, but override it when you want to pull data from a different load case.  
   • Downstream Grouping Logic  
     – In more complex DBMERG scenarios (as described in Section 2.6 “GRP – Group Assignment”), these load-case indices are combined with “NDIV” and multiple GRP blocks to distribute or replicate results across varied element groups.  Correct use of NO and NOS ensures your data flows into the intended load cases before any grouping logic is applied.

By understanding the role of each column and the interplay of NO (new LC) and NOS (old LC), you can precisely control how DBMERG reads from one set of load-case results and writes them into another, either on a one-to-one basis or in bulk via your grouping directives.

The table summarizes the three primary parameters used by the DBMERG utility’s GRP (group‐assignment) feature. Each row defines one parameter (Item), its purpose (Description), any measurement Unit (all are dimensionless here), and the Default value if the parameter isn’t explicitly supplied. These parameters work together to control how elements or nodes from a “project” database are mapped onto elements or nodes in a “source” (additional) database, based on simple arithmetic grouping rules.  

1. Item “NO”  
   • Description: Group number for source data.  
   • Unit: – (dimensionless)  
   • Default: “!” (mandatory; the user must provide this value when defining a GRP block)  
   • Role: Specifies the group index assigned to each master (project) element or node. Internally, DBMERG divides each element’s ID by NDIV (if provided) and uses the remainder (modulus) to determine its group. Elements are only merged or “mirrored” with target elements that share the same group index.

2. Item “NOS”  
   • Description: Group number for target data.  
   • Unit: – (dimensionless)  
   • Default: same as NO (if you don’t supply NOS, DBMERG assumes the target group index equals the source group index)  
   • Role: Defines which group in the source database will feed results into each group of the project database. If NOS is set differently from NO, you can map one group of source elements onto a differently numbered group in the project database.

3. Item “NDIV”  
   • Description: Group divisor.  
   • Unit: – (dimensionless)  
   • Default: “*” (no division; the entire element number is taken as the group index unless overridden)  
   • Role: Controls group‐number calculation by integer division. DBMERG computes group numbers by dividing the element/node ID by NDIV and then using integer modulus arithmetic. This lets you specify repeating patterns—for example, if NDIV=100, then IDs 1001–1003 all yield a modulus of 1–3 and can be paired with source IDs 101–103 in the same three‐member group.

Usage Notes and Examples (from the surrounding DBMERG documentation):  
- If only NO is provided (and NOS defaults to NO), a one‐to‐one mapping occurs between matching group indices in project and source databases.  
- Specifying multiple GRP blocks (each with its NO, NOS, NDIV) allows you to set up hierarchical or fallback assignments. DBMERG uses the first valid mapping it encounters. This mechanism can implement default transfers last, and more specific transfers first, without conflict checking.  
- Beam elements get paired only when their physical length matches exactly, even if group indices align.  
- When node numbering rules differ between the two databases, you can define separate GRP blocks with distinct NO/NOS/NDIV settings to handle each region or component.  
- The “!” default for NO forces users to consciously assign a source group, preventing accidental full‐database merges without explicit grouping logic.

By clearly defining NO, NOS, and NDIV, RAG vector‐store ingestion scripts can index and retrieve vector embeddings that correspond to specific element groups and their merged result sets. This table is critical for automated parsing of DBMERG input decks and for downstream semantic search or retrieval in a knowledge‐driven engineering workflow.

LC
 Any action of DBMERG will use the selected load cases only. With input of NOS you may copy results to other load case numbers.
 In combination with the grouping of the elements you may assign in different blocks results of different elments of the same load case to different load cases of the same element. The default NO=NOS is only posssible, if you have two data bases open.
 2.6 GRP – Group Assignment
 GRP
 For the transfer of data elements of the project base will be assigned to elements of the source database. Without any input a 1 to 1 assignement is in effect.
 The group number is given as division of the node or elementnumber by NDIV. Two elements will be assigned to each other if the modulus will be the same and the group numbers follow the specified assignment. In DBMERG you may define completely other groups than those which are defined in the database.
 Beam elements, however, will be assigned to each other only if the beam length is also identi- cal.
 If the node numbers do not follow the same rules as the elements, you have to use to seperate blocks with different assignements.
 This feature can be used to multiply the properties of prefabricated parts.
 Example:
 In the project data base are the elements 1001, 1002, 1003 as well as 1101, 1102, 1103 and 2001, 2002, 2003 defined. In the additional data base are the Elements 101, 102, 103 defined. Input of
 +PROG DBMERG HEAD GRP NO 9999 NOS 0 END
 defines the assignments:
 1101 := 101 , 1102 := 102 and 1103 := 103
 Elements 1001 to 1003 resp. 2001 to 2003 are without assignment. The results of elments 101 to 103 will be assigned to the elements 1101 to 1103.

1101 := 101 , 1102 := 102 and 1103 := 103. Elements 1001 to 1003 resp. 2001 to 2003 are without assignment. The results of elments 101 to 103 will be assigned to the elements 1101 to 1103..
 Input of:
 +PROG DBMERG HEAD GRP NO 10 NOS 1 NDIV 100 GRP NO 11 NOS 1 NDIV 100 END
 defines the assignments:
 1001 < = 101 , 1002 < = 102 und 1003 < = 103
 1101 < = 101 , 1102 < = 102 und 1103 < = 103
 and will thus copy the results multiple to the elements. And finally
 +PROG DBMERG HEAD GRP NO 9999 NOS 1 NDIV 100 END
 will assign:
 1001 < = 101 , 1002 < = 102 und 1003 < = 103
 1101 < = 101 , 1102 < = 102 und 1103 < = 103
 2001 < = 101 , 2002 < = 102 und 2003 < = 103
 For the data transfer the first valid assignment is used, multiple assignements are not checked, which allows to define a general default as last assignment, while more specific ones are defined first.

The table summarizes the set-up parameters for the “NODE” operation, which governs how nodal results are selected, scaled, and copied for specified load cases and groups. It is organized into four columns—Item (the parameter name), Description (its function), Unit (its measurement units, if any), and Default (the built-in starting value)—and is intended for use when configuring result extraction in a post-processing or data-export step.

1. Overall Context  
   • Context line: “NODE  For the selected load cases and groups the results will be copied.”  
   • Purpose: Control which nodal results are active (or deactivated), choose among result types, and apply scaling factors to forces, displacements, and moments before copying.

2. Column Definitions  
   • Item: The keyword used in the input deck or API to specify each option.  
   • Description: A concise explanation of what that keyword controls.  
   • Unit: The physical unit or an indicator (“—” for unitless) of the parameter value.  
   • Default: The value assumed if the user does not supply an override.

3. Parameters

   A. TYPE (Unit: LIT, Default: ALL)  
   • Governs which categories of nodal results are to be worked on (i.e., copied or deactivated).  Available literal values:  
     – NONE: Turn off all result types.  
     – ALL: Enable every available result type (default).  
     – LINK: Forces arising from kinematic constraints.  
     – LOAD: Applied nodal loads.  
     – DISP: Nodal displacements.  
     – REAC: Reaction forces/support reactions.  
     – VELO: Nodal velocities.  
     – ACCE: Nodal accelerations.  
     – MPHY: Multiphysics or user-defined results.

   B. FX (Unit: —, Default: 1.0)  
   • Scale factor applied to all X-direction displacements or forces when copying results.  

   C. FY (Unit: —, Default: FX)  
   • Scale factor for Y-direction displacements/forces; defaults to the FX value if unspecified.

   D. FZ (Unit: —, Default: FY)  
   • Scale factor for Z-direction displacements/forces; defaults to whatever FY is set to.

   E. FXX (Unit: —, Default: FZ)  
   • Scale factor for X-axis rotations or moments; inherits from FZ unless explicitly changed.

   F. FYY (Unit: —, Default: FXX)  
   • Scale factor for Y-axis rotations/moments; defaults to FXX.

   G. FZZ (Unit: —, Default: FYY)  
   • Scale factor for Z-axis rotations/moments; defaults to FYY.

4. Usage Notes  
   • By chaining defaults (FY → FX, FZ → FY, etc.), the user can set a single factor for all translational or rotational components.  
   • Explicitly setting TYPE to NONE suppresses any nodal output, while ALL ensures comprehensive data capture.  
   • The unit “LIT” for TYPE indicates that it takes a literal keyword rather than a numeric value.

This structured parameter set allows fine-grained control over exactly which nodal results are output and how they are scaled, making post-processing and data export tasks flexible and configurable.

NODE
 For the selected load cases and groups the results will be copied.

The table shown defines the set of input parameters used by the “BEAM” module when copying analysis results for selected load cases and groups. It is structured in four columns—Item, Description, Unit and Default—and covers two categories of inputs: a “TYPE” selector for result categories, and seven scaling factors for various internal force and moment components.

1. Columns  
  • Item: The mnemonic identifier for each parameter.  
  • Description: A brief explanation of what each parameter controls.  
  • Unit: The physical units or notation in which the parameter is expressed (here all are either a literal code or dimensionless).  
  • Default: The value assumed if the user does not supply an override.

2. TYPE (Item = TYPE)  
  – Purpose: Specifies which categories of results will be activated (i.e. copied to the output) for the chosen load cases and load case groups.  
  – Allowed values (literal codes under “Unit” = LIT):  
     • NONE – Deactivates all result categories.  
     • ALL – Activates all available result categories (default).  
     • LOAD – Pure loading data (external load vectors).  
     • FORC – Internal forces and bending moments.  
     • STIF – Element stiffness matrices.  
     • EIGE – Secondary (eigenmode) forces and moments.  
     • STRE – Stresses computed from internal forces.  
     • REIN – Reinforcement results (e.g. steel area in RC beams).  
     • TEND – Tendon (prestressing) forces and moments.  
  – Default: ALL (i.e. everything is copied unless a narrower selection is specified).

3. Force and Moment Scaling Factors  
   After choosing which result types to copy, the user can optionally apply uniform scaling factors to the seven fundamental beam-result components. Each factor is dimensionless (Unit = “—”) and defaults in a cascading fashion so that if one is left unspecified it inherits the value of its predecessor in the list.  

  • FN – Factor for normal (axial) forces.  
     – Unitless multiplier applied to axial force results.  
     – Default = 1.0 (no scaling).  

  • FVY – Factor for shear forces in the local y-direction.  
     – Default = FN (inherits the axial‐force factor unless explicitly set).  

  • FVZ – Factor for shear forces in the local z-direction.  
     – Default = FVY (inherits the y-shear factor).  

  • FMT – Factor for torsional moments (twist).  
     – Default = FVZ (inherits the z-shear factor).  

  • FMY – Factor for bending moments about the local y-axis.  
     – Default = FMT (inherits the torsion factor).  

  • FMZ – Factor for bending moments about the local z-axis.  
     – Default = FMY (inherits the y-bending factor).  

  • FMB – Factor for warping (bimoment) moments.  
     – Default = FMZ (inherits the z-bending factor).  

4. Usage Context  
  In practice, an engineer working with the BEAM analysis tool will first choose the TYPE code to select only those result categories of interest (for example, forcing only “FORC” and “STRE” if only internal forces and stresses are needed). Once the relevant result streams are activated, the set of FN…FMB factors can be used to apply any required magnification or scaling (to account for load combinations, safety factors or unit conversions) before the results are written out or passed on to post‐processing routines.  

Overall, this table neatly encapsulates all switch-type and scaling inputs required to control and modulate the output of beam element results in a single, easy-to-reference form.

BEAM
 For the selected load cases and groups the results will be copied.

The table shown (often referred to as the “TRUS” card in many finite‐element or structural‐analysis input decks) defines two configuration parameters—TYPE and FN—that control which results are generated for truss elements and how axial forces are scaled. It is organized into four columns (Item, Description, Unit and Default) and contains the following rows:

1. Item: TYPE  
   • Description: “Type of results to work on.” This parameter accepts a literal code (LIT) that tells the solver or post-processor which subset of truss results to compute or display. Five possible string values are supported:  
     – NONE: Deactivates all result types (no output).  
     – ALL: Selects every available result type (forces, moments, stresses, etc.).  
     – LOAD: Requests only loading information (e.g., applied loads).  
     – FORC: Requests internal forces and bending moments in the truss elements.  
     – STRE: Requests design stresses (axial stresses, allowable stress checks, etc.).  
   • Unit: LIT (literal string)  
   • Default: ALL  

   By defaulting TYPE to ALL, the software will compute and return every category of truss result in one run. If the analyst only needs, for example, stress checks (STRE) or internal forces (FORC), setting TYPE accordingly can reduce output volume and post-processing time.

2. Item: FN  
   • Description: “Factor for normal forces.” This is a scalar multiplier applied to the computed axial (normal) forces in each truss element. It allows the user to inflate or reduce forces globally—often used for load factors, safety factors or parameter studies.  
   • Unit: — (dimensionless)  
   • Default: 1.0  

   With FN at its default of 1.0, no scaling is applied and the forces come through exactly as solved. If, for instance, an engineer needs to amplify every axial force by 10 percent, FN can be set to 1.1; to apply a 5 percent reduction, FN would be 0.95.

• Column “Item” names each parameter.  
• Column “Description” explains purpose and permitted values.  
• Column “Unit” denotes whether the parameter is a literal string (LIT), dimensionless, or has other units.  
• Column “Default” gives the value assumed when the parameter is omitted.

The table is organized into four columns—Item, Description, Unit and Default—and is used in the context of the QUAD module for copying finite‐element results (for selected load cases and groups).  It governs two primary aspects of postprocessing:  
  1. Which types of results are activated or suppressed (the TYPE block)  
  2. What multiplicative factors are applied to individual force and moment components (the factor block)  

----------------------------------------------------------------  
1. TYPE (Item = TYPE, Unit = LIT, Default = ALL)  
This entry controls exactly which result categories the QUAD routine will “work on” (i.e., copy, scale, or output).  Under TYPE, you can specify one or more of the following literal codes.  If you set TYPE to NONE, all output is deactivated; setting it to ALL turns on every available result channel.  The intermediate codes enable only specific data streams:  
  • BLOA  – free‐load vectors (loads applied outside the element stiffness)  
  • FLOA  – element‐level loading details (e.g. pressure, temperature loads)  
  • FORC  – internal forces and moments (section forces m-xx, m-yy, m-xy, etc.)  
  • NFOR  – nodal forces (resultant reaction or internal nodal loads)  
  • ERRO  – error estimator (global or local error norms from adaptive analysis)  
  • BEDD  – foundation stresses (soil‐spring reactions beneath elements)  
  • CRAC  – crack‐orientation output (e.g. angle of crack path in concrete shells)  
  • YIEL  – nonlinear shell stress parameters (e.g. von Mises indices)  
  • STRE  – stresses in elements (plane stress, plane strain tensors)  
  • NSTR  – stresses in nodes (averaged or extrapolated stresses)  
  • ERRS  – error estimator based on stresses (stress‐driven error metrics)  
  • DESI  – design stress results (allowable vs. actual stress comparisons)  
  • NDES  – design stresses in nodes (nodal design check values)  
  • REIN  – reinforcement forces (rebar tension/compression in concrete)  
  • NREI  – reinforcement results at nodes (extrapolated or averaged)  
  • TEND  – tendon forces (prestressing tendons in post‐tensioned elements)  

Using TYPE effectively lets you include or exclude whole families of output.  For instance, setting TYPE = FORC+STRE would yield internal force/moment diagrams together with element stress fields.  

----------------------------------------------------------------  
2. Scaling Factors  
Below TYPE, the table defines eight scalar “factors,” each of which multiplicatively scales a particular component of the element result.  The Unit column is blank (dimensionless), and the Default column shows a chained set of fallback values so that if you don’t explicitly set a given factor it inherits the previous one in the list.  The recommended workflow is to leave these defaults alone—misusing them to “suppress” torsional (m-xy) or shear terms can mask real load effects.  

  FMX   – bending‐moment factor for m-xx  
           Default = 1.0  

  FMY   – bending‐moment factor for m-yy  
           Default = FMX  

  FMXY  – torsional‐moment factor for m-xy  
           Default = FMY  

  FVX   – shear‐force factor for q-x  
           Default = FMXY  

  FVY   – shear‐force factor for q-y  
           Default = FVX  

  FNX   – membrane‐force factor for n-x  
           Default = FVY  

  FNY   – membrane‐force factor for n-y  
           Default = FNX  

  FNXY  – membrane‐shear‐force factor for n-xy  
           Default = FNY  

Because each default points back to the preceding factor, setting just FMX to 1.2 will automatically scale every moment, shear and membrane component by 1.2—unless you override an individual factor explicitly.  If you need to treat one component differently (e.g. magnify shear but leave bending at unity), you would override FVX or FVY after setting FMX.  

----------------------------------------------------------------  
Contextual Note (from QUAD documentation)  
“Factors should not be misused to suppress torsional moments.”  In practice, that means you should not simply set FMXY to zero to hide twisting effects; instead, exclude FORC from TYPE or postprocess selectively.  This preserves the integrity of the structural response and avoids inadvertently ignoring potentially critical loading scenarios.

QUAD
 For the selected load cases and groups the results will be copied. Factors should not be missused to supress torsional moments.

This table defines the primary input parameters used when copying and post-processing stress‐related results in the BRIC module (“for the selected load cases and groups the results will be copied”). It is organized into four columns—Item, Description, Unit, and Default—and two logical blocks: the result TYPE selector and the stress scaling factors (FSX/FSY/FSZ/FTAU).

1. Columns
   • Item  
     – The keyword or parameter name that the user must provide in the input deck.  
   • Description  
     – A brief narrative explaining the purpose of the parameter, and in the case of TYPE, the list of valid sub‐options.  
   • Unit  
     – The measurement unit or data type expected. A dash (“–”) indicates a dimensionless scalar. “LIT” implies a literal token or string.  
   • Default  
     – The value assumed if the user omits the parameter. Some defaults refer to other items, establishing a dependency chain.

2. Block A: TYPE (Unit = LIT, Default = ALL)  
   The TYPE parameter governs which kinds of results are activated for copying or further analysis. It accepts one of seven literal codes:  
     • NONE   – Deactivate all values; no result fields will be processed.  
     • ALL    – Select all available result types (this is the DEFAULT).  
     • LOAD   – Include raw loading data only.  
     • STRE   – Extract stresses evaluated at element centroids.  
     • NSTR   – Extract stresses evaluated at nodal points.  
     • ERRS   – Compute and return an error estimator derived from stress fields.  
     • MPHY   – Include multiphysics coupling results (thermal, fluid, electro-mechanical, etc.).  

   Use TYPE to finely control output size and focus: for instance, choosing STRE+NSTR to compare element‐ vs. node‐based stress fields, or ERRS to drive adaptive refinement.

3. Block B: Stress Scaling Factors (Unit = –)  
   These four parameters apply uniform multipliers to stress results before storage. They are dimensionless by design but can be used to scale units or apply safety factors.  
     • FSX (Default = 1.0)  
       – Multiplier for σₓ (normal stress in the X direction). Default of 1.0 leaves the raw result unchanged.  
     • FSY (Default = FSX)  
       – Multiplier for σᵧ (normal stress in the Y direction). By default it inherits FSX’s value, ensuring uniform scaling unless explicitly overridden.  
     • FSZ (Default = FSY)  
       – Multiplier for σ_z (normal stress in the Z direction). Inherits FSY by default, creating a cascading default chain (FSZ←FSY←FSX).  
     • FTAU (Default = FSZ)  
       – Multiplier for τ (shear stresses). Inherits FSZ by default, so in the absence of user input all stress components scale together by FSX.  

   If a user provides only FSX, then FSY, FSZ, and FTAU automatically match FSX. To apply different scalings for different axes or shear, each factor can be set individually.

4. Usage Notes  
   – The TYPE selector should typically be the first parameter in a BRIC block to define the scope of copied results.  
   – Scaling factors are optional and default to unity scaling. They can double as unit conversion factors (e.g., from Pa to MPa by setting FSX=1e-6).  
   – The cascading defaults reduce verbosity: specifying FSX alone suffices for uniform scaling. If axis‐specific safety margins are needed, override FSY, FSZ, and/or FTAU explicitly.

By structuring inputs this way, the BRIC module achieves both flexibility in selecting result sets and simplicity in applying uniform or differentiated stress scaling.

BRIC

The table under examination is organized into four columns—Item, Description, Unit and Default—and defines three parameters (rows) related to extrusion settings in a structural or finite‐element context. Below is a detailed breakdown of its structure and semantics:

1. Overall Layout  
   • Column “Item” gives a short code or keyword by which each parameter is identified in input decks or APIs.  
   • Column “Description” provides a human‐readable explanation of what the parameter controls.  
   • Column “Unit” indicates the measurement dimension or data type expected for each parameter’s value.  
   • Column “Default” supplies the value assumed when no explicit input is provided.

2. Row 1: TYPE  
   • Item code: TYPE  
   • Description: “Type of extrusion.” This entry specifies which geometric or coordinate‐manipulation procedure is applied when extruding a 2D cross section into a 3D element.  
   • Unit: LIT (literal), meaning the input is a string or keyword rather than a numeric quantity.  
   • Default: PCA. By default, a “cyclic permutation of coordinate axes” (abbreviated PCA) is used. In practice, PCA causes the original local axes to be rotated or permuted in a cyclic fashion as the section is extruded, which can be important for maintaining material or geometric orientations.  
   • Additional context: “cyclic permutation of coordinate axes” clarifies that PCA stands for a specific re‐indexing of axes (for instance x→y, y→z, z→x) as the extrusion proceeds along the third dimension.

3. Row 2: STYP  
   • Item code: STYP  
   • Description: “Subtype.” This parameter allows further classification within the chosen extrusion type. Different subtype values can trigger specialized internal routines or boundary conditions in the solver.  
   • Unit: [–] (dimensionless), indicating a unitless numeric code—commonly an integer or floating‐point flag.  
   • Default: 1.0. A default subtype value of 1.0 typically corresponds to the most common or standard variation of the extrusion procedure. Users may override it with other values (e.g., 2, 3, etc.) to invoke alternative behavior.

4. Row 3: TREF  
   • Item code: TREF  
   • Description: “Reference depth for sectional forces at 2D‐system.” When sectional forces (axial, bending, shear) are computed in a 2D cross‐section and then extruded into 3D, TREF designates the depth coordinate used as the baseline or “zero” reference plane. This affects how internal forces are distributed along the element’s depth.  
   • Unit: [m] (meters), reflecting a physical length measurement.  
   • Default: 1.0 m. If no custom reference depth is provided, the system assumes a unit depth of one meter for all sectional force calculations.

Usage Notes for RAG/Vector‐Store Ingestion  
• Each Item code serves as a unique key for indexing in a vector‐based retrieval system.  
• The “Description” field should be broken into searchable keywords—e.g., “extrusion type,” “coordinate axes,” “subtype,” “reference depth,” “sectional forces,” “2D‐system.”  
• Units and Defaults can be stored as metadata attributes or numeric vectors to support range‐based queries (e.g., find all parameters with default = 1.0 m) or type‐based filters (e.g., select all literal‐type settings).  
• The PCA note is particularly important as a disambiguator—PCA might otherwise be confused with “principal component analysis,” but here it clearly means “cyclic permutation of coordinate axes.”

Below is a structured, detailed description of the provided table, suitable for use in a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) vector store. It explains the purpose of the table, its schema, and the semantics of each parameter. Context from the accompanying note (“ECHO – Output of the program is a protocol of the transferred or assigned data volume. The content is controlled by the record ECHO.”) is woven in wherever relevant.

1. Table Purpose and Context  
   • This table defines two configuration records—OPT and VAL—that govern the content and granularity of the ECHO output.  
   • The ECHO record itself produces a “protocol” (i.e., a logged report) detailing the volume of data that has been transferred or assigned by the program.  
   • By setting these two parameters, a user or calling routine can specify which subsets of data appear in the report (OPT) and how much detail each selected subset carries (VAL).

2. Overall Schema  
   The table is composed of four columns, each playing a distinct role:  
   – Item: The short mnemonic or keyword used in the program’s input to select or modify behavior.  
   – Description: Human-readable explanation of the item, including any permissible enumerations.  
   – Unit: Indicates the data type or literal format expected. Here, “LIT” denotes that the input is a literal text string.  
   – Default: The value assumed by the program when no explicit override is provided.

3. Detailed Field Descriptions  

   Item: OPT  
     • Description: “Select an option.” Controls which portions of the data‐transfer protocol appear in the ECHO output.  
       – FULL: Include all available information in the report.  
       – LC: Restrict output to specified load cases only.  
       – GRP: Restrict output to specified groups only.  
     • Unit: LIT (expects one of the literal strings FULL, LC, or GRP).  
     • Default: FULL (if the user does not set OPT explicitly, the system assumes they want the complete protocol).

   Item: VAL  
     • Description: “Value of option.” Defines the level of verbosity or detail for the subset chosen by OPT.  
       – NO: Suppress output entirely (no protocol is generated for the chosen subset).  
       – YES: Produce normal or standard output (default verbosity).  
       – FULL: Produce extended or highly detailed output for the chosen subset.  
     • Unit: LIT (expects one of the literal strings NO, YES, or FULL).  
     • Default: YES (the system generates standard‐level detail when VAL is not specified).

4. Usage Notes  
   • Combined, OPT and VAL form a two‐dimensional control matrix:  
     – E.g., OPT=LC and VAL=FULL would yield an extended report, but only for the designated load cases.  
   • Omitting either setting causes the system to fall back to its default behavior (OPT=FULL, VAL=YES), ensuring that by default a concise protocol of all transfers is produced.  
   • Both parameters must be supplied as uppercase literal tokens; any deviation (lowercase, misspelling) may be rejected or ignored by the parser.

5. Integration in RAG  
   • When ingested into a vector store, this description can help retrieval systems answer queries such as:  
     – “What are the possible verbosity levels for the ECHO report?”  
     – “How do I restrict the output to groups only?”  
   • Keywords to index: OPT, VAL, ECHO, FULL, LC, GRP, NO, YES, detailed output, verbosity control, default values.
